items.title: What is MakeACS?
items.text:
MakeACS is an open-source, modular, low-cost system that makes managing your makerspace, FabLab, or teaching shop easier. The system incorporates machine-level access control, training administration, statistics collection, and shop-management resources like audit logs, maintenance tracking, and inventory control to simplify your workflows. MakeACS can be further augmented via standard API interactions, allowing it to interface with systems like PaperCut, 3DPrinterOS, and student enrollment databases.

MakeACS is 100% open-source, modifying it and hacking it is encouraged! Hardware and firmware is licensed under the CERN-OHL-S 2.0 license, and software is licensed under AGPL-3.0. All source files, documentation, and resources can be found on the MakeACS GitHub, at https://github.com/MakeACS.

MakeACS is developed by the Rochester Institute of Technology's Student Hall for Exploration and Development, with contributions from the open-source community. Learn more about the Student Hall for Exploration and Development at www.rit.edu/shed.

items.title: MakeACS by the Numbers
items.text:
MakeACS currently handles all operations of 7 makerspaces at RIT, with work underway to incorporate MakeACS at other shops at RIT. At least two other universities are also in the process of integrating MakeACS into their shop operations.

As of November 2026, over 200 pieces of MakeACS hardware have been deployed, amassing over 150,000 interactions with makers. The MakeACS server at RIT has administered over 62,000 trainings to the 8,700 registered makers. To date, more than 15,000 unauthorized equipment access attempts have been stopped with MakeACS.

items.title: Table of Contents
items.text:
1. Introduction: You are here!
  2. Website: A centralized place to learn more about the shop and its resources.
  3. Trainings: Train users on how to properly use equipment.
  4. Access Control: Control and monitor who is using equipment.
  5. Shop Management: Make it easier to do your job.
  6. Statistics & Logging: Understand usage trends in your shop.
  7. System Price: How much does MakeACS cost?

items.title: 2. Website
items.text:
The MakeACS website is the public face of your shop! Users can come here to learn more about equipment, take trainings, and see important information like hours and equipment availability. For staff, it is the main control interface and how all shop management resources are accessed.

The MakeACS homepage at the RIT SHED Makerspaces

items.title: Public Information
items.text:
The website is visible to users even before they log in, with lots of useful information;

  • Facility hours, with support for special-case hours and differing hours for different areas.
  • Announcements with an integrated call-to-action link.
  • Facility information such as locations, links to maps, etc.
  • General machine information, and links to manuals, guides, etc.
  • Real-time equipment availability, to see if what you are looking to use is free.
  • A publicly-available REST API for getting the hours, announcements, etc. for integration into other systems and websites.
  • Upcoming events, pulled via API from systems like Eventbrite.

Additionally, the website generates and serves pages for the hours, announcements, and events that can be constantly displayed on screens around the facility. These screens will automatically update as changes are made to the website, and handle anti-burn in image shifting. They are designed to be extremely easy to display, so a cheap Raspberry Pi Zero connected to the back of the TV can handle it.

Check it out yourself; make.rit.edu/app/display/hours/36

Upcoming Events, Hours, and Announcements Displays

items.title: Logging In (SSO)
items.text:
MakeACS supports user login via SSO, implementing Shibboleth SAML 2.0. This allows users to log in with already-existing university or institution credentials, and also means MakeACS does not have access to any sensitive information, such as passwords.

When a user logs in, SSO information is automatically pulled and updated on the user's MakeACS account. By default, this includes their first and last names, institution username/email, and preferred pronouns. MakeACS can be configured to gather more information based on SAML attributes, such as a user's role in the institution (student, staff, alumni, etc.), home department, graduation year, etc., for use in statistics.

Additionally, user accounts can be restricted based on SSO attributes. For example, RIT does not permit alumni to use the makerspaces, but they still retain an RIT SSO account. If an alumni signs in to MakeACS, their account is flagged and put in an archived state, so they can no longer access equipment. See user restrictions for more information.

A user's preferred name and pronouns are readily accessible by staff, so they can properly address users.

User info visible to staff, pulled from SSO

items.title: Equipment Information
items.text:
The MakeACS website's primary purpose is to help users find information about equipment. Equipment can represent just about anything in a facility - discrete equipment, general tooling, or services. To help logically organize equipment, the entire MakeACS facility can be split into top-level makerspaces, each of which can contain multiple rooms, that each then contain equipment.

There is no limit on the number of makerspaces, rooms, or equipments in a MakeACS website. For very large facilities, there is a search bar in each makerspace to help filter down options.

The "General Makerspace" contains a room called "3D Printing", with 2 different equipments.

Each piece of equipment gets a card, that contains the name of the equipment, a brief (markdown-supported) description of its use, an image, a link to the training checklist, and a link to further information, such as a manual or docs page. If fitted with access control hardware, the real-time availability of equipment will be displayed as well.

Looks like the vinyl cutter is already in use!

Tip

There can be multiple instances of a piece of equipment, which all share the same training requirements. This is a useful way to group, for instance, 3 laser cutters under one "Laser Cutter" equipment card and training checklist.

items.title: Reservations
items.text:
MakeACS equipment, by default, is first-come, first-serve. For specialized, long-duration, or in-demand equipment, MakeACS implements a reservation system. Equipment can be designated as self-reservable, where any trained user can book an appointment, or staff-reservable, where users can see the availability on a calendar, but need to work with staff to reserve it.

My trainings are not done, so the "RESERVE" button is greyed out.

Reservation data is anonymous; users cannot see who else has a reservation, just that a date is unavailable. Restrictions can be placed on when a user can make a reservation, and how far in advance it must be scheduled.

Reservations must be approved or denied by staff. To help staff manage reservations, an automated Slack message or email can be sent on a new reservation request.

items.title: Customization
items.text:
The MakeACS website is fully customizable without the need for any programming skills! Custom themes can be designed in a graphical editor, which can either be enforced on all users, or provided as an option. This enables a dark/light mode, seasonal overlays, and small easter eggs! Even the website's logo and name can be changed as part of a theme.

Tip

Images with a transparent background are automatically given a white background in any dark theme, so the subject of the image is still clearly visible.

Dark mode is a very popular theme that many users opt for.

MakeACS also incorporates a link shortener and QR code generator, allowing the creation of shortened URLs based on the MakeACS website URL. This creates a better user experience with easier-to-type URLs, and a sense of familiarity using the same URL as the rest of the shop's resources. As an example, RIT uses

make.rit.edu/link/policies

to direct users to makerspace policies, instead of the much harder to type

docs.make.rit.edu/%E2%80%8BPolicies%20%26%20Guidances/Makerspace%20Policies/

items.title: 3. Trainings
items.text: Once a user learns about equipment on the MakeACS website, we should put their knowledge to the test! MakeACS has an integrated training system, that ties into the access control system, to lock equipment usage behind trainings and sign-offs.

items.title: Training Configuration
items.text:
Managers can assign training requirements to a specific piece of equipment, or to an entire room (such that it is required by all equipment in that room). Trainings can be reciprocal, for instance finishing the "Drill Press Safety" training for a drill press in the wood shop can also count for a drill press in the metal shop.

Edits to trainings go out immediately, and do not necessarily invalidate previous passes of a training. Trainings can also be archived to temporarily hide them, and remove them from all equipment.

Managers can also set a training's expiration policy. Trainings can be configured to require a regular re-completion to maintain access, or a training can be good forever once passed. When a training is nearing expiration, users will get an email reminding them to renew it.

Users can see training requirements for each piece of equipment via a "Training Checklist" on the website. If a training has an expiration date, the expiration can be checked here as well.

The MakeACS website also serves a mobile-friendly version of the training checklist, designed to be accessed via QR code at the machine in case a user finds they do not have access. This page will also diagnose other access restriction issues, such as a user having a hold on their account.

items.title: Online Trainings
items.text:
The primary form of trainings associated with MakeACS are online trainings. These can be taken at any time by users, and support both desktop and mobile-friendly formatting.

Trainings can be comprised of (markdown) text, images, videos, PDFs, and multiple-choice single-answer or multi-answer questions. Trainings are created and edited via a simple training editor baked into the MakeACS website, accessible to managers.

An example of an embedded video training, pulled from YouTube

Managers can configure the required pass rate for an online training to be considered complete. To help users score better, questions can be configured with a hint and affirmation, given to the user as feedback when they complete a training.

To prevent brute-force completions, a user who fails a training 3 times in a day has that specific training locked for 24 hours. This is recorded for audit purposes, and can be overridden by staff if needed.

Info

The completion of a training can also be used to trigger an API call - for instance at RIT, completing the training on how to use 3DPrinterOS grants your 3DPrinterOS account access to submit prints!

items.title: In-Person Checks
items.text:
The second form of trainings associated with MakeACS are in-person checks. These require a user to come in-person, and work with a trainer to demonstrate competency, review the function of the equipment, etc.

In-person checks can be configured to be completable by any staff within the equipment's space, or by a select list of designated trainers.

Tip

Staff cannot perform an in-person check on equipment they themselves do not have the check completed on. Furthermore, staff are blocked from signing off their own account's in-person checks.

In-person checks are not available for sign-off until the user has completed any relevant online trainings.

To help users prepare for (and to remind staff of what topics to cover in) an in-person check, each piece of equipment can optionally have a link set with information on the in-person check. This link would be found in the training checklist, along with online trainings.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
MakeACS's primary feature is the machine-level access control system. When paired with the MakeACS website, this enables locking equipment access behind trainings, tracking usage statistics, automatically generating maintenance tickets based on usage, and displaying real-time availability on the website.

MakeACS hardware is a module, shared-bus system; multiple individual components can be interconnected to tailor the hardware to the application at hand. By combining different card readers, switches, and accessories, thousands of possible setups can be achieved.

When installing, each component is self-contained, and only connected by a simple low-voltage cable. In most cases, there is no specialized training or skills required to install MakeACS hardware. Any configuration that is needed can be done through a graphical user interface from any Windows computer.

MakeACS hardware contains multiple automated safety and integrity checks, to detect and defeat attempts at tampering with, bypassing, or otherwise damaging the hardware.

An AC Power Switch and a Core are the most common deployment.

items.title: The Core
items.text:
The Core is the heart of a MakeACS deployment. It is where the end-user interacts with the system, and is how the deployment communicates with the website.

All Cores are equipped with both a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi radio and a 100Mbps Ethernet connection to communicate with the website. All traffic to and from the Core is TLS 1.2 encrypted, so it can be put onto your facility's main network without security concerns. In the event of a network outage, the Core can operate off of internal offline lists of approved users for up to a month.

User identification in MakeACS is designed around repurposing already-issued ID cards, such as student IDs or membership cards. This means fewer things for your users to have to remember when they come in to make. Supported cards include:

  • NFC (13.56MHz), ISO/IEC 14443A, MIFARE (Classic, Ultralight, Ultralight C, Plus, DESFire), NTAG
    • Can identify by ISO UID or by decrypting secure application data (such as a student ID number)
    • Hardware supports smartphone- or smartwatch-based NFC identification as well.
  • RFID (125KHz), FSK (HID and HID-compatible, up to 39 bytes), ASK (EM Microelectronic and compatible)
    • Can be configured to use unique card number or facility code + card number for user identification

Once a user has been identified and the server authorizes them to use the equipment, the session is kept alive in one of two configurable ways;

  • Tap: Works like a traditional access control card reader, tapping the ID card will start a session of a pre-set length. Tapping again refreshes the countdown.
  • Insert: Requires the card to remain inserted into the MakeACS Core to continue a session duration indefinitely, ensuring constant operator presence.

When I am done with the equipment, I simply remove my card.

The Core has a basic RGB LED and buzzer for communicating state, but also has an open-ended connection interface to allow for a display module. This can show a user why their access was denied, show announcements (such as notifying users the shop is closing soon), or for equipment in tap mode, how long remains on a session.

Tap you ID to activate the paint booth. The display will show you how long you have remaining in your session.

The Core can also be used as a sign-in reader to a space. This is useful for collecting statistics of the number of people who enter the space and when, and can also be used to enforce users checking in at the front desk before using equipment for the day.

If you do not sign in for the day, equipment will not unlock for you!

items.title: The Switch
items.text:
The Switch is the part of the access control hardware that actually controls access. There are a number of switches developed for MakeACS, with different strategies for integrating with a wide variety of equipment. Multiple switches can also be used together, to form more complex access control setups all from a single card reader.

In most cases, the switch is also where the MakeACS deployment harvests power from, so there is usually no need for an additional power cable or connection. This allows the deployment to be mounted wherever is best for accessability and ergonomics, with no need to worry about proximity to an outlet.

items.title: AC Power Switch
items.text:
The AC Power Switch is by far the most popular MakeACS switch. It simply goes inline between the outlet on the wall and your equipment's power cable. There is no need for any invasive in-machine wiring or doing your own AC connections.

The AC Power Switch is rated for highly inductive loads, and can handle a sustained 20 amps of current. This makes it suitable for anything from a sewing machine to a bandsaw.

The switch will monitor for any faults such as over-temperature or blown fuses, and can automatically restrict access and notify staff. The AC Power Switch can also be configured to not allow a machine to be activated if it is detected to be in the "on" state, to prevent unexpected startups. Conversely, the AC Power Switch can be configured to give a warning if a session ends while equipment is detected to still be in use, so the user has a chance to restart the session and prevent issues.

To prevent bypassing or tampering, the AC Power Switch has an optional plug lock, to secure the equipment's plug in place.

The AC Power Switch, mounted to the base of a drill press.

items.title: USB Hub Switch
items.text:
For a lot of complex equipment, the easiest way to control access to it is by locking down its computer. This strategy works great on laser cutters, water jets, and CNC machines. For this, the USB Hub Switch is a great fit. The switch will activate or de-activate 4 downstream USB ports for keyboards, mice, USB drives, etc.

The USB Hub Switch has a 5th downstream USB port that is connected when the switch is off, which can be used to automatically execute a cleanup script. For instance at RIT, when a user removes their ID card from a laser cutter's computer, it will go through and force-close all windows, make sure the user is logged out of any accounts, etc., before restarting the laser cutter software to give a blank slate to the next user.

items.title: Relay Switch
items.text:
For applications that require more direct integration with equipment, the Relay Switch is the best choice. The relay switch provides galvanically isolated dry contacts, that can be integrated with any arbitrary power or signal to control a piece of equipment. Common examples include interrupting an interlock or e-stop loop, or switching a larger purpose-installed contactor for very large loads like a welding station.

There are 3 variants of the Relay Switch in MakeACS:

  1. The Signal Relay Switch has special gold-plated contacts, allowing it to work with small digital signals, like those from a microcontroller. It has 2 sets of NC and NO contacts, so you can switch multiple signals in parallel. Each contact pair can handle up to 0.5A at 125V.

  2. The DIN Relay Switch is rated for 250V at 5A, for integration with larger electrical cabinets. It is usually used to drive a larger contactor for high-current or high-voltage loads, such as a welding station or large woodworking equipment.

  3. The DIN Controller is similar to the DIN Relay Switch, but with 5 independent channels. This allows you more control over how a system is controlled. For example at RIT, this switch is used on the paint booth: the lights, fan, and heater are on 3 separate channels, so anyone can turn on the fan and lights, but only those who are authorized can turn on the burner.

items.title: Other Components
items.text: Beyond simply controlling access, MakeACS supports additional accessories in a deployment, to further augment the capabilities. Here are some examples of these;

items.title: Temperature Monitor
items.text:
The temperature monitor allows an arbitrary temperature probe to be attached to a deployment, that can be used to lock out access if a temperature gets too cold or too hot.

At RIT, this is used to ensure the paint booth is not drawing in too much cold outside air, chilling the entire makerspace.

items.title: Indicator Light
items.text: To help users see equipment availability, this add-on allows the attachment of a standard Andon light tower, which can show deployment state.

items.title: Laser Fume Monitor
items.text:
This add-on integrates with the Epilog Laser fume extractor control interface, and will monitor for and report any faults related to the filters or the air assist supply line. If either is found to be malfunctioning, the equipment is locked out automatically.

The fume extractor failed to start, so the system is put into lockout.

items.title: Hobbs Timer
items.text: While MakeACS automatically tracks usage time based on the total time on, this add-on allows for a specific signal to be used for hours tracking. This is useful on something like a CNC, where maintenance tasks should be based on spindle run-time, versus machine on-time.

items.title: Buddy System Enforcer
items.text:
This add-on lets two Cores control one deployment, in one of three modes. This enables hardware-enforcement of the buddy policy on high-risk equipment, or more complex user authorization setups.

  • AND Mode: Both Cores need an approved user present to activate the equipment. This ensures 2 trained users are present at all times. The training requirements for each of the Cores can be different as well, to ensure a specially-trained staff member is present, for instance.

  • OR Mode: Either Core needs an approved user to activate the equipment. This allows trained users to hand off equipment without disrupting its operation.

  • AND-OR Mode: Both Cores need an approved user to activate, but then either one can keep it online. This is useful on equipment where you want staff to check over things before the user starts running, but once it is approved they can work on their own.

items.title: Blast Gate Controller
items.text: This add-on enables MakeACS to open blast gates based on what equipment is in use. This ensures maximum suction to where it is needed, and prevents excessive wear on the vacuum system when nothing is in use. It is designed for use with iVac automated blast gates, but can work with any generic 12v blast gate system.

items.title: Deployment Examples
items.text: Below are some examples of how MakeACS is deployed at RIT.

items.title: AC Power Switch
items.text:
The AC Power Switch is by far the most common switch. RIT uses it on the following machines, to name a few;

  • Bernina 475, 590, E16, L460, Q20
  • Weller soldering iron
  • Metcal soldering heat gun
  • Roland RS-24 Vinyl Cutter
  • Bantam CNC mill
  • Laguna bandsaw, belt sander, drum sander, jointer
  • Powermatic drill press
  • Jet bandsaw, edge sander
  • Generic panel saw
  • Generic rotary grinding/sanding tool

items.title: Haas CNC Machines
items.text:
All Haas CNC machines produced after 2014 ship with an NGC (Next Generation Controller). This controller has a dedicated auxiliary E-stop plug, intended for connecting a robot or other automation system. This connection can instead be connected to a Relay Switch.

Power for the system can come from the spare 110V outlets found inside most Haas electrical cabinets.

Source: HaasCNC.com

items.title: Fablight Laser Cutter
items.text:
The Fablight Laser Cutter has an spare interlock loop in an access panel on the left side of the machine, intended for use with a tube-extension add-on. A Relay Switch interrupting this connection is read as a door-open fault, and the machine will not move or fire the laser until a card is present.

Power for the system can come from open USB ports inside the electrical cabinet.

items.title: ProtoTrak Mill
items.text:
KMX-controller ProtoTrak machines have an auxiliary E-stop plug in the back of the machine, labeled "EURO E-STOP". By default, it ships with a jumper head on it that connects pins 1-6, 2-4, 3-5, and 7-8-9. Interrupting the 2-4 connection with a Relay Switch puts the controller in an emergency lockout state, making the machine inoperable but without losing any of the parameters saved in the controller.

On KMX machines with a power knee, RIT also installs an AC Power Switch, so that the knee's power is cut when a card is not present.

items.title: Epilog Laser Cutter
items.text:
Epilog lasers can take up to a minute to start up, so cutting their power is not ideal. Instead, at RIT access control restricts use of the computer used to send jobs to the laser, by interrupting their keyboard, mouse, and exposed USB ports with a USB Hub Switch.

This has the added benefit of running an automatic cleanup script when a user is done with the computer, ensuring all their work is closed and all accounts are logged out, so every user has a clean-slate experience.

items.title: OMAX Waterjet
items.text: OMAX waterjets are intended to be constantly connected to an operator computer. By interrupting the computer's keyboard and mouse with a USB Hub Switch, the user cannot activate the pump or start a cut. The benefit of this is that it does not interfere with any critical interfaces, such as the E-stop or feed hold buttons, meaning they are always readily available in the event of an emergency.

items.title: Generic Lab Computers
items.text: For lab computers with software or licenses that do not play well with individual user accounts, a USB Hub Switch controlling access to a computer can help keep a record of users, and reset the computer to a known state after each use, with the help of software like Deep Freeze.

items.title: DIY Hardware
items.text: The MakeACS bus interface and MQTT API are standardized, and can be found in the MakeACS Hardware Standards. Compliance with these standards allows you to develop your own MakeACS hardware that is interoperable with all other MakeACS devices.

items.title: 5. Shop Management
items.text:
To make operations smoother, MakeACS integrates a number of shop management tools, available only to staff and managers.

Note

Managers are an elevated permission level, anything that is noted as something a staff can do, a manager can do as well.

items.title: Tool Loaning
items.text:
For high-value, high-risk, or in high-demand resources that would not be suitable for a traditional reservation calendar, the website implements a loan-out tracking system. Users can check out equipment with a staff member, and return it when complete. If a user forgets to return equipment for more than 24 hours, a flag is raised to follow up with the user.

Upon loaning or returning equipment, staff can be presented with images and/or formatted text, to verify they are giving the correct item and everything is as it should be. Staff can note damage or issues upon return for investigation. Current loan or damage states, and historical usage data, can all be used in statistical analysis.

items.title: History
items.text:
To help staff better understand what is happening in the shop, a real-time history page is visible. This shows every action taken within the space in chronological order, with the ability to search and filter it.

The history embeds useful click-through links, to help staff more efficiently complete their jobs. For example, the audit log "Jim Heaney has signed into the Atrium Makerspace" has a click-through to Jim Heaney's user account, so staff can quickly access information on them.

This data can be used to draw statistical conclusions on shop operations as well.

Names of actual users redacted from screenshot

items.title: Equipment State
items.text:
Staff have the ability to see the real-time state of all equipment in the space, including the current user if in-use. Staff also have the ability to remotely set the state of the equipment to either lock it out, such as in the event of needing maintenance, or locking it always on, such as for a workshop or training. Staff only have the ability to lock on equipment while in the space (enforced by physical sign-in), and only for equipment they themselves are trained on.

Note

If a staff forgets to reset an always-on machine, it is automatically returned to the idle state every morning at 4am. Equipment in the locked-out state remains that way, even through a power cycle, until lifted by a staff.

This view also Hobbs time, see statisitics for more info.

items.title: Inventory Control
items.text:
The MakeACS server has an integrated inventory management system, for tracking consumables, spare parts, and for-sale items. Staff can add or remove inventory via the normal MakeACS website, or via special mobile-optimized pages that are intended to be on QR codes directly attached to the inventory. Inventory can also be managed through an API, to enable more complex integrations.

Managers can set categories, price points, and restock policies on a per-item level. When inventory goes below a set threshold, the system can automatically send a Slack or email notification to trigger a re-order.

Inventory items can have images or notes attached to them, to help staff identify them or to have re-order information on hand in one centralized location.

Time to order more filament!

items.title: Maintenance Logs
items.text:
To aid in tracking equipment issues, a maintenance logging system is available to all staff. Staff can open reports with issues they find, and attach images to assist in future diagnostics. Which staff claim/close a ticket, how long the ticket took to close, and how often tickets of a set severity level are registered against a piece of equipment are all logged for statistical analysis.

Tip

The At-Machine Training QR Codes, when scanned by a staff, provide a mobile-friendly maintenance report page! This makes it easy to report issues when staff spot them, rather than having to go to a computer.

When a maintenance ticket is generated, it can be used to trigger an automatic email or Slack message, to keep maintenance staff informed about ongoing issues.

In addition to reported issues, the MakeACS server can automatically generate tickets, based on two different criteria;

  • Time-based tickets are opened a set interval after their last iteration was closed. An example is a weekly reminder to check the eye wash stations.

  • Usage-based tickets are opened after a set amount of on-time from the MakeACS hardware. An example is a ticket to change the oil on the waterjet every 50 hours.

Maintenance logs that are marked with a high severity can be configured to automatically lock out equipment and deny all access attempts.

"SERVER" tickets are for scheduled/regular maintenance

items.title: User Restrictions
items.text:
In the event that staff find a user acting in an improper or dangerous way in the makerspace, they have the ability to place a restriction on their account. This will flag their account for review by a manager, and stop them from using any equipment in the makerspace until it is resolved.

Managers have the ability to place a hold on a user's account, which stops them from using all equipment under MakeACS, notifies staff if they attempt to sign in to a makerspace, and locks down their view of the website. Even when removed, a permanent record of a hold is left on the user's account.

Staff and managers can also see and edit notes on a user's account, to help log information for other staff.

items.title: Organizations & Finances
items.text:
Managers have the ability to credit user accounts with a virtual currency - Construct Credits - that can be used to purchase items from inventory, or as part of automated payment integrations with systems like 3DPrinterOS, supplementing funds from traditional sources like PaperCut or Atrium.

In addition to being able to issue such credits to individual users, managers can create organization accounts and issue credits to them. This allows research labs, student teams, etc. to operate under one financial umbrella, rather than having to designate a single point-of-contact.

items.title: 6. Statistics & Logging
items.text:
Every action in MakeACS is logged and kept in perpetuity.The history page allows for searching for one-off information, such as identifying what user was using a piece of equipment at a specific time, or all MakeACS data can be accessed via SQL query for use with a larger system like Grafana, such as plotting average number of users per month.

Info

MakeACS logs can be kept for as long as there is server space to store them. See system price for more information.

items.title: Equipment/Space Data
items.text:
Data on equipment, sign-ins, tool loans, etc. can all be used to identify trends in utilization. Collected data includes;

  • Equipment session start time and duration
  • Sign-in date and time
  • Tool loan out and return times
  • Time of, reason for equipment access denied

Below are some examples of this data in use;

Plotting sign-ins per day can help identify times of the year when the shops are more used, and may need more support.

By averaging the number of sign ins per hour per day of the week, we can identify times of the day that may require more staffing;

Seeing if excessive numbers of access attempts are being denied, and if so for what reason, can help you understand if there is sufficient user training on how the system works.

items.title: Training Data
items.text:
Training data logged for analysis includes;

  • Pass rate per training
  • Correct rate per question in the training
  • Datetime of training completion

This allows the identification of troublesome trainings and questions within them for refinement, or for identifying trends in training interests as a proxy for equipment interest. Exporting specific training results allows you to run reports on users who completed a training to allow it to be used as a class assignment.

Training data is also collected in regards to staff, for instance being able to track how many in-person competency checks a staff performs, which equipment they perform the most in, etc.

items.title: User Data
items.text:
Tip

Does your institution have specific policies regarding user data handling? No problem. MakeACS can be hosted by your institution directly to comply with regulations.

User data can be collected from SSO attributes, or collected manually from the user durning sign-up. Additional data is collected and associated with the user by MakeACS:

  • Most recent sign-in
  • Currently-used theme
  • Sign-up date
  • Most recent ID card update
  • Completion datetime of trainings
  • Usage of equipment

This user-centered focus on data allows you to develop narrative stories of the user's experience with the shop; did they start by coming in to use one piece of equipment then branch out as needed? Or did they plan ahead, complete all trainings on all equipment, then get to work?

items.title: Website Data
items.text:
Basic information related to the MakeACS website is logged, such as sign-up balks (a user started making an account, but gave up).

For more in-depth website usage data, MakeACS supports Google Analytics. Simply enter your tracking key to get real-time and historical data on traffic sources, popular pages, bounce rates, average time per page, and much more!

items.title: 7. System Price
items.text:
One of the main development goals of MakeACS was to create a system that did not cost much to implement nor maintain. Below is a breakdown of the costs of implementing MakeACS;

Note

All prices listed are for the price of materials and BOM items, and assumes you are doing any assembly/installation yourself.

TL;DR / BLUF:

  • About $150-200 per machine for access control hardware (one-time purchase).
  • Under $20 per month for the MakeACS website, less if you have a smaller shop.

items.title: Hardware Cost
items.text:
The Access Control Hardware is the most expensive part of a MakeACS deployment, an average setup comes out to around $200 per machine.

Let's look at an example; what would it take to put MakeACS on all five sewing machines in our textiles shop? Sewing machines plug directly into the wall, so simply putting an AC Power Switch inline is sufficient. Each machine will also need a Core, so we can read the ID of the user sewing.

items.title: Circuitry
items.text:
All electrical circuitry in MakeACS is designed to be easy to order, with BOM and Gerber files being optimized for use by JLCPCB and similar assembly houses. Further savings can be realized by doing partial or full assembly yourself.

If we assume worst-case and have boards 100% assembled and shipped to us;

  • 5x AC Power Switch: $324
  • 5x NFC Core: $356
  • International Shipping, Customs and Duties: $65

Electronics Total: $745 (149 per machine)

items.title: Wiring
items.text:
MakeACS uses standard HD15 cables to interconnect components. The suggested cable is one made by Amphenol Cables on Demand, but any quality brand should work. In our case, we'll opt for 5-foot cables, so we can mount the AC Power Switch out of the way, while still having the card reader easily accessed by the user.

  • 5x Amphenol Cables on Demand HD15 5' (CS-DSDHD15MM0-005): $80.30
  • Digikey Shipping & Tariffs: $64.08

The AC Power Switch also needs a cable to connect to the wall power. Any generic C13 (computer) power cable will work, but a 14AWG one rated for 15A is suggested to cover all load-cases.

  • 5x 14AWG C13 Power Cable (Generic, Amazon): $60

Wiring Total: $204.38 (40.88 per machine)

items.title: Enclosures
items.text:
All MakeACS hardware enclosures are optimized for 3D printing, and can be printed on any printer you already own to save money! Alternatively, the components are designed with few critical tolerances, so it is cheap and easy to have them manufactured by a 3rd party.

For the AC Power Switch, it is suggested to use a UL94-V0 rated filament, to add an extra layer of thermal protection surrounding the electronics.

All 3D printed components for 5 AC Power Switches and 5 NFC Cores cost less than $30 if you have your own 3D printer.

items.title: Mechanical Hardware
items.text:
MakeACS standardizes around very common metric M3 and M4 hardware, that can be bought in inexpensive bulk packs from Amazon, McMaster-Carr, or your local hardware store. This brings the hardware cost to only $10 for our example.

The one somewhat specialized mechanical component needed would be the DIN rail mounting plate the NFC Core uses to attach itself to its base, a DRB48-1. A 5-pack of these is only $15 on Amazon, though.

items.title: Miscellaneous
items.text:
Some other small miscellaneous things will be needed;

  • 2A and 20A glass fuse for AC Power Switch: $2
  • Dual-Lock or similar to mount the NFC Core and AC Power Switch: $5
  • A USB-B cable for configuring the NFC Core (if you do not already have one): $5

items.title: Total
items.text:
Adding up the above, the total cost to deploy MakeACS hardware on 5 machines is only $203 per machine

The best part? It gets cheaper the more you buy, with bulk discounts especially present on the electronics. If we opted for 30 sets of hardware instead, it drops the price to under $130 per machine!

Adding additional features is also cheap and easy. For instance, adding a display to the Core is only $30 per unit. Such upgrades can also come down the road thanks to the modular nature of the MakeACS hardware, so there's no need to make the decision right away.

items.title: Server Cost
items.text:
What good is the hardware being cheap if it costs a ton to keep the server running? The MakeACS server is designed to be extremely resource-conscious, requiring very little to run. We wouldn't recommend it, but you can easily run it off of a Raspberry Pi tucked away in the corner of the shop!

In most cases, hosting through a vendor like Heroku is the best option. Below is the configuration used by RIT, supporting over 8000 users across 7 makerspaces;

  • Dyno (Heroku Cedar Basic): $7 per month: The "computer" part of the server, that handles actually running the website.
  • Datastore (Heroku Postgresql Essential 2), $20 per month: Handles database storage of all information. This plan allows full data logging for 50 years before database size constraints kick in.
    • For smaller facilities, or if you regularly delete data older than 3 years, you can get away with plans as little as $5 per month!

Some additional costs come into play if your scale gets very large;

  • AWS Cloudfront CDN: Handles storing and serving images, documents, videos, etc. embedded into the website. Kept separate from Heroku to save costs. $0 per month unless you are exceeding around 10,000 website sessions per month. Beyond that, it costs around $1 per 10,000 monthly visits to the website.
  • Mailgun: The part of Heroku that handles sending emails. Free for up to 400 emails per day, 401-50,000 emails per day costs up to $19 per month. Emails can be batched and sent out over time to keep under the 400 email limit, to avoid paying for the mail services.
  • Grafana Hosting: If you want to use Grafana for visualizations, but do not want to have to host it yourself, you can integrate it into Heroku via Stackero for up to $19 per month.

So for most applications, the cost ends up below $30 per month!

Keep in mind: MakeACS is open-source. If your facility or institution already has server hosting capacity, you may be able to run MakeACS off of that for $0 per month!
